questions.q: Why is caseworker-to-caseworker sharing in this scenario stricter than typical role-hierarchy sharing?
options: Because Public Sector Solutions does not support role hierarchy at all
Because case data is scoped to "assigned to me," not "anyone sharing my role," so a peer caseworker should not see another caseworker's cases by default
Because every caseworker must have an identical role to every other caseworker
Because supervisors are not allowed to see any case data under this design
questions.explain: The scenario specifically requires scoping below "same role sees everyone's records," which is why assignment-based private sharing, not broad role-based visibility, is the right mechanism for caseworker peers.

questions.q: What additional mechanism does the design use to prevent a housing caseworker from discovering that the same household has an open child-welfare case?
options: Nothing extra is needed beyond standard role hierarchy
Deleting the child-welfare case from the system entirely
Giving every caseworker access to every program by default, then relying on training not to look
An explicit cross-program consent gate / restriction rule that must be affirmatively satisfied before visibility crosses a program boundary
questions.explain: Because all three programs share one platform, an explicit additional gate is needed on top of ordinary case-assignment sharing — simply not granting access isn't enough when the underlying sharing model would otherwise expose it.

questions.q: Why does child welfare get the strictest visibility treatment of the three programs in this scenario?
options: Because child welfare cases involve the least sensitive data of the three programs
Because child welfare cases are never assigned to any caseworker
Because there are real legal reasons certain parties must never be shown that a child-welfare case exists at all, not just reduced visibility
Because housing assistance is legally required to always be more visible than child welfare
questions.explain: This scenario specifically calls for a case that can be legally invisible to a specific person, not merely less visible — a stronger requirement than ordinary restricted sharing.

questions.q: Why must the data-residency decision (citizen data staying within the state's borders) be made at the platform/infrastructure layer before data is created?
options: Because the commitment is about where data physically lives and is processed, and retrofitting that after records already exist in the wrong region doesn't fix the data already created there
Because residency only matters for data that's older than five years
Because Hyperforce regions can be changed instantly at any time with no consequence
Because residency requirements only apply to citizen-facing portals, not internal case data
questions.explain: Residency is a foundational, early decision precisely because it governs where data is created and processed from the start — treating it as an afterthought leaves already-created data in the wrong place.

questions.q: Why shouldn't the citizen-facing Experience Cloud portal use the same role-hierarchy mechanism internal staff use for their own visibility?
options: Because Experience Cloud users cannot be granted any Salesforce access under any configuration
Because citizens should actually have broader access than internal caseworkers
Because role hierarchy automatically applies to portal users with no configuration needed

Because the internal role hierarchy was never designed to safely bound an external citizen's access, so citizen visibility should instead be scoped narrowly through sharing sets tied to their own submitted records
questions.explain: Citizen access needs a narrower, purpose-built scoping mechanism (sharing sets tied to the citizen's own records), since reusing the internal staff hierarchy for an external audience risks exposing more than intended.
